Large-scale micro-aerobic digestion studies at municipal water resource 
recovery facilities for process-integrated biogas desulfurization 
Norbertus Joannes Richardus Kraakman a,b,*, Israel Diaz b, Maria Fdz-Polanco b, Raul Mu˜noz b 
a Jacobs Solutions, One Glass Wharf, Bristol BS2 0EL, United Kingdom 
b Institute of Sustainable Processes, University of Valladolid, Doctor Mergelina s/n, 47011 Valladolid, Spain   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Biogas desulfurization 
Energy recovery 
Hydrogen sulfide 
Micro-aeration 
Micro-aerobic digestion 
Sludge valorization 
A B S T R A C T   
Biogas generated from anaerobic digestion processes typically requires gas conditioning including hydrogen 
sulfide removal before it is used on-site to generate electricity and heat or before upgrading to biomethane for gas 
pipeline distribution or vehicle fuel. Experiments of process-integrated micro-aeration in three different large- 
scale sludge digesters (effective volume 2450 m3, 3250 m3 and 3300 m3) were undertaken at municipal 
wastewater treatment plants and compared with large-scale applications reported in literature. This work dis­
cusses critical process parameters, advantages, and potential limitations of micro-aerobic digestion in compar­
ison with other commonly used biogas desulfurization methods. It shows that high H2S reduction in the biogas 
can be obtained and that the H2S reduction is dependent not only on the air injection rate and location, but also 
on the digestion activity identified by the volumetric biogas production. Reliability testing of typical micro- 
aerobic upset scenarios and long-term micro-aerobic digester operation as part of this study provided deeper 
insights in the MA process that could also provide valuable input to what operational, maintenance and safety 
measures should be considered when applying micro-aeration in large-scale digesters. The large-scale micro- 
aerobic digestion trials demonstrated that the hydrogen sulfide concentration in the biogas can be controlled 
using minimal plant upgrades, contributing to the sustainability and economic efficiency of the energy recovery 
process of waste sludge digestion at water resource recovery facilities.   
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is extensively used to process organic 
wastes such as sewage sludge and source segregated organics (SSO), 
including agricultural waste materials and the organic fraction of 
municipal solid waste. Anaerobic digestion is more commonly used in 
recent years because of its potential to generate renewable energy from 
diverse feedstocks [1]. AD may also be used to divert organic wastes 
from landfills, thus minimizing the operational costs and environmental 
impacts of landfills. Moreover, AD is increasingly used as the core waste- 
to-renewable-energy process of sludge management at large municipal 
water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs), while it stabilizes the waste 
sludge, reduces potential pathogens, and turns the sewage sludge into a 
natural fertilizer [2]. 
The produced biogas typically requires conditioning before it is used 
to generate energy, typically in internal combustion engines, turbines 
and boilers, or before its upgrading to biomethane for gas pipeline dis­
tribution or use as a vehicle fuel. Elevated concentrations of hydrogen 
sulfide (H2S) in the biogas are often a limitation for downstream pro­
cessing of the biogas as it creates maintenance related corrosion prob­
lems in combustion engines, occupational health issues and the release 
of SOx in flue gases, which entails harmful environmental effects and are 
subject to air permit restrictions [3]. The H2S concentration in biogas 
varies from a few hundred to up to 10,000 ppmv, depending on the 
sulfate inlet concentration and the amount of bioavailable sulfur com­
pounds in the feedstock. The maximum H2S concentration when biogas 
is used as fuel in cogeneration engines for combined heat and power 
(CHP) production is typically <100 ppmv, depending on the manufac­
turer, and <5 ppmv for biomethane gas pipeline distribution or use as a 
vehicle fuel [4,5]. 
Elevated H2S concentrations in biogas are usually obtained by iron 
salts dosing into the digester or by applying conventional physical/ 
chemical end-of-pipe biogas desulfurization technologies (i.e., wet 
scrubbing using water/caustic/hypochlorite or iron oxide–based ad­
sorbents). These methods are relatively expensive due to ongoing 
operational costs and may cause high environmental impacts [6]. Cost-

effective and more environmentally friendly alternatives have recently 
emerged that include biotechnology (i.e., aerobic or anoxic biotrickling 
filtration) or physical-chemical combinations with biotechnology (i.e., 
caustic scrubbing followed by biological oxidation) as discussed by 
Dumont [7]. However, these technologies are still hampered by their 
high investment costs and their generated byproducts that need further 
processing or disposal (i.e., sulfuric acid and/or elemental sulfur slurry). 
A simple and economical alternative is a process-integrated 
biochemical method of removing H2S from the biogas called micro- 
aeration (MA) and involves the dosing of a small amount of air or oxy­
gen during the digestion process. The MA process takes place inside the 
digester and the bacteria responsible for sulfide oxidation are already 
present in the feed sludge. Micro-aerobic conditions during anaerobic 
digestion have been studied at bench-scale and proven to be an effective 
method for reducing H2S concentrations in the produced biogas [8–10]. 
MA has been researched and used in agricultural biogas plants, but 
rarely tested at the typical larger sludge digesters at municipal WRRFs. It 
has been demonstrated in Europe in a few large-scale sludge digesters at 
WRRFs, with H2S removal efficiencies of >90 % in most cases [11,12]. 
MA may also improve the degradation of organic matter (volatile 
suspended solids) and enhance methane production [13]. In addition, 
there is evidence that MA can enhance the stability of the digestion 
process, lower the foaming potential of the digested sludge, improve 
sludge dewaterability and reduce the chemical oxygen demand (COD) 
and dissolved sulfide concentration in the digested sludge centrate 
[13–16]. The potential drawbacks of MA include methane dilution 
(when relatively large amounts of air/oxygen are injected), and an 
accumulation of elemental sulfur in downstream gas pipes or flame ar­
restors [17]. Inhibition of the methanogenesis may also occur when too 
much air/oxygen is injected [18,8,19]. 
A comprehensive process understanding is necessary under larger- 
scale conditions, which can facilitate the scale-up and optimization of 
the MA process to obtain high quality biogas, maintain a stable digestion 
process, and eliminate unexpected maintenance and operational costs of 
the micro-aerobic digestion process. Operational and design parameters 
such as the amount of air dosed, the air dosing location and the liquid 
conditions, have shown to be important in bench-scale studies [18–24]. 
Nevertheless, additional digester design and operating parameters may 
be critical when scaling-up the MA process to successful implementation 
in large-scale digestion processes. This can include the type of organic 
feed material, the reactor type (e.g., internal configuration and volume, 
headspace volume, and/or reactor sludge mixing method) and the 
operational conditions. 
The aim of this study is to investigate the biogas desulfurization 
performance in three different large-scale sludge digesters using MA. In 
addition, the impact of sudden changes in micro-aeration rate and 
typical digestion upset conditions are studied to better understand the 
MA process reliability. The findings are compared with bench-scale and 
other large-scale studies reported in literature to discuss critical process 
parameters and potential limitations in comparison with other 
commonly used biogas desulfurization methods, as well as opportunities 
to be considered when scaling-up MA for the waste-to-energy digestion 
process of sludge management at large municipal WRRFs. 
2. Materials and methods 
MA technology was studied over a period of multiple months in 
large-scale digesters at WRRFs in North America all different in terms of 
reactor size, organic loading rate, H2S concentration in the biogas and/ 
or sludge mixing method. The waste sludge fed into the digesters was in 
all cases a mixture of primary sludge (PS) and waste activated sludge 
(WAS). The H2S concentrations in the biogas in the period immediately 
before or after the MA test were approximately 5500 ppmv, 1000 ppmv 
and 2250 ppmv for Case Studies #1, #2 and #3, respectively. Sludge 
mixing in the digesters was done either by means of sludge recirculation 
through pumping (Case Study #1 and #3) or through biogas 
recirculation (Case Study #2). The average organic loading rate (OLR) 
was 2.1, 3.3 and 2.4 kgVS m−3
r d−1 during the evaluation period for Case 
Studies #1, #2 and #3, respectively. 
2.1. Case Study #1 
MA technology was implemented over a period of ten weeks in a 
large-scale 20-meter diameter digester with an effective volume of 2450 
m3. The waste sludge fed into the digester was about 105 m3 d−1, after 
gravity thickening. The feed sludge was a mixture of PS and WAS, in a 
volumetric ratio of approximately 1 to 1, with a TS concentration of 
about 6.0 % (w/w) and a VS content that was ~79 % of TS. The sludge 
was digested under mesophilic conditions at a hydraulic retention time 
of approximately 22 days. 
Mechanical sludge recirculation was used for sludge mixing inside 
the digester with an average recirculation flowrate of 850 m3 h−1, which 
resulted in an average sludge turn-over rate of ~3 h. The recirculated 
sludge was returned to the digester either near the bottom of the digester 
reactor or near the top of the digester just below the sludge surface using 
alternating valves (the discharge location was switched every 4 h from 
top to bottom). The OLR was ~2.1 kgVS m−3
r d−1 during the evaluation 
period. The H2S concentration in the biogas prior to the large-scale MA 
period ranged between 5000 and 6000 ppmv. 
During the MA tests ambient air (compressed service-air) was 
injected with fine bubble air injection nozzles in the sludge recirculation 
pipe downstream of the sludge recirculation pump (see Supplementary 
Fig. S-1 for the developed and implemented test set-up). The biogas H2S 
concentration was monitored under different air dosing conditions. In 
addition, the impact of micro-aeration on the volatile solids reduction 
(VSR) was measured. The impact of sudden changes in micro-aeration 
rate on the biogas H2S concentration was also evaluated. The flowrate 
of air injected and the H2S concentration in the biogas were measured 
daily. Digested sludge samples were taken daily for analyses and sludge 
feed, sludge recirculation rate and biogas production were measured 
continuously. 
2.2. Case Study #2 
MA technology was also studied over a period of six months in a 
large-scale digester at WRRF in a 21-meter diameter digester (effective 
volume of 3250 m3). The waste sludge flowrate fed into the digester was 
~180 m3 d−1. The digester was fed with PS and WAS (volumetric ratio of 
approximately 1 to 1), which were co-thickened in dissolved air flotation 
tanks (DAFTs). The sludge exhibited a TS concentration of ~6.0 % (w/ 
w) and a VS content that was ~87 % of TS. The sludge was digested 
under mesophilic conditions with a hydraulic retention time of about 18 
days, with the digester being mixed via gas recirculation. The H2S 
concentration in the biogas prior to the large-scale MA period ranged 
between 1000 and 1200 ppmv. 
The air injection set-up during the large-scale micro-aerobic diges­
tion tests in shown in Fig. S-2. Ambient air (compressed service-air) was 
initially injected in the recirculating sludge heating line just downstream 
of the sludge feed point of the digester. The large-scale pilot test 
continued injecting the air in the bottom of the digester using an existing 
25-milimeter pipe after isolating one of the twelve biogas feeder pipes 
from the digester gas mixing system. Finally, the desulfurization per­
formance was monitored under different micro-aerobic air dosing con­
ditions during continuous and discontinuous (1 h on–1 h off) gas 
recirculation. 
The amount of air injected and the H2S concentration in the biogas 
were measured daily. Digested sludge samples were taken daily for 
analyses and sludge feed, sludge recirculation rate and biogas produc­
tion were measured continuously. Sulfur analyses were performed of the 
feed sludge and the digested sludge of the micro-aerated digester during 
Case Study #2 to generate a sulfur mass balance of the micro-aerobic 
digestion process. The sulfur analyses were performed during the

2.3. Case Study #3 
Finally, MA technology was studied over a period of about three 
months in a third large-scale digester (16-meter diameter with an 
effective volume of 3300 m−3). The waste sludge flowrate fed into the 
digester was ~111 m3 d−1, after gravity thickening. The feed sludge was 
a mixture of PS and WAS, in volumetric ratio of approximately 1 to 1, 
with a TS content of ~4.8 % (w/w) and a VS content that was ~87 % of 
TS. The sludge was digested under mesophilic conditions designed 
under a hydraulic retention time of approximately 30 days. 
Mechanical sludge recirculation was used for sludge mixing inside the 
digester with an average recirculation flowrate of 749 m3 h−1, which 
resulted in the sludge in the digester being turned over through recircu­
lation pumping on average once every about 4.4 h. The recirculated 
sludge was taken from the bottom middle of the digester and returned near 
the top of the digester at ~2 m below the sludge surface at four evenly 
distributed locations 1 m from the wall to create a continuous swirl of 
digesting sludge inside the digester. The OLR was ~2.4 kgVS m−3
r 
d−1 
during the evaluation period. The average H2S concentration in the biogas 
prior to the large-scale MA test ranged between 2000 and 2500 ppmv. 
Ambient air (compressed service-air) was injected with fine bubble 
air injection nozzles in the sludge recirculation pipe downstream of the 
sludge recirculation pump. Fig. S-3 shows the air injection set-up that 
was implemented during the large-scale digester testing. The desulfur­
ization performance was monitored under different micro-aerobic air 
dosing conditions. 
The amount of air injected and the H2S concentration in the biogas 
were measured daily. Digested sludge samples were taken daily for 
analyses and sludge feed, sludge recirculation rate and biogas produc­
tion were measured continuously. The flowrate of air injected and the 
H2S concentration in the biogas were measured daily. Digested sludge 
samples were taken daily for analyses while sludge feed, sludge recir­
culation rate and biogas production were measured continuously. 
2.4. Process upsets responses 
Different possible process changes and potential process upset sce­
narios were investigated to gain an improved understanding of the 
reliability of the process-integrated MA under large-scale operations. 
Reliability is the combination of robustness and resilience, where 
robustness reflects the capacity of a system to maintain its functionality 
when subjected to changes. The resilience is the rate at which a system 
returns to its original state after being perturbed. Several digestion or 
micro-aeration process changes or upset scenarios were investigated, 
including a sudden MA-air injection stop (all Case Studies), MA-air in­
jection rate overdose (Case Study #1), intermittent sludge gas mixing, a 
gas mixing blower failure (Case Study #2) and a sludge recycle pump 
failure directly followed by a digester feed pump stop (Case Study #3). 
2.5. Analytical procedures 
Sludge characteristics such as pH, alkalinity, total solids (TS) content 
and volatile solid (VS) content were measured daily using standard 
methods [25], while biogas production and sludge feeding rate were 
measured continuously using electromagnetic flowmeters. The air in­
jection rate was measured using a flowmeter (Dwyer, RMD 0.5 – 600 
scfh, 100 psi) and daily recorded. The H2S concentration in the biogas 
was measured daily using either Dr¨ager tubes or a handheld biogas 
analyzer (BIOGAS 5000, QED Environmental Systems, Inc., USA) and 
verified by taken biogas samples with silonite canisters for Fixed Gas lab 
analysis by standard method EPA 3C and the total reduced sulfur 
analyses by standard method ASTM-D-5504. 
For sulfur analyses, the sludge samples were collected by filling a 
plastic bottle quickly and completely without getting sludge in much 
contact with air. Concentrated sodium hydroxide was added to the 
samples to raise the pH to a minimum of 8.5 and directly centrifuged to 
obtain a liquid fraction and a solid fraction. The liquid and solids frac­
tion samples were stored in the fridge and shipped cold the next day to 
an analytical lab (ALS Environmental, Tucson, Arizona). Both the liquid 
and solid fractions were analyzed on different sulfur constituents (sul­
fides, sulfate and total sulfur). The sulfide concentration was analyzed 
according to EPA standard method M9030, the sulfate concentration 
was analyzed in accordance with EPA standard M9056 and the total 
sulfur concentration was analyzed as per ASTM methods D1552/D4239. 
ORP measurements were carried out using a handheld ORP meter 
(Hach HQ40d multimeter) during Case Study #2. In addition, an online 
ORP meter (Hach pHD sc with platinum electrode in stainless steel flow 
cell) was also tested in the bypass line of the sludge recirculation pump 
using a special ORP probe injection piece from the manufacturer. 
3. Results 
3.1. Case Study #1 
After introducing the air into the sludge on day 0, the H2S concen­
tration in the biogas slowly started to drop over about a week (Fig. 1). 
The initial air dosing rate was 4 m3 h−1, which was increased to 8 m3 h−1 
after 3 weeks. Air dosing was further increased in several smaller steps 
over a period of 5 weeks to about 14 m3 h−1. At day 0, two fine bubble 
air injection nozzles were used, at day 26 three fine bubble air injection 
nozzles were used and finally at day 56 all the six installed air nozzles 
were in operation. 
The H2S concentration in the produced biogas ultimately dropped 
over a period of 8 weeks by >80 % from about 5000 ppmv to <1000 
ppmv. After stopping the MA on day 60, the H2S concentration increased 
back to about 5000 ppmv. The presence of MA in the anaerobic digestor 
showed no negative effects on organic matter removal, or biogas pro­
duction when the amount of air injected was limited to less than about 
13.6 m3 h−1. Biogas was produced under mesophilic conditions and its 
production rate was on average 4508 Nm3 d−1 (average of three di­
gesters using one biogas flowmeter installed in the common outlet gas 
header) or 0.8 m3 per kgVS under a digester loading rate of 2.14 kgVS m−3
r 
d−1, which didn't change during the test period of 8 weeks. 
The pH of the sludge was 7.3 ± 0.15 without any pH control, while 
the operational temperature was kept on average at 33 ± 4 ◦C. The 
digested sludge during the test period had an average TS content of 2.5 
± 0.2 % (w/w). While methane production rate remained basically 
unchanged when introducing MA, the VS/TS ratio of the digested sludge 
dropped in this case by a few percent from about 66.6 % without MA to 
about 63.6 %. 
3.2. Case Study #2 
Directly after initiating the air supply into the digester's sludge 
recirculation line, the H2S concentration in the biogas dropped within 
one week from about 1000 ppmv to about 500 ppmv (Fig. 2). After three 
weeks at an aeration rate of 2.5 m3 h−1, which entailed an H2S con­
centration of ~400 ppmv, the air injection rate was slowly increased 
stepwise. This ultimately resulted in a biogas H2S concentration of ~200 
ppmv when 5.7 m3 h−1 of air was injected. 
The testing was continued by dosing air injected in the bottom of the 
digester compared to the previous phase where the air was injected into 
the sludge recirculation line. During this test, the H2S concentration in 
the biogas dropped within three weeks from about 1000 ppmv to 400 to 
500 ppmv. After 3 weeks (day 21), the air injected was increased, which 
did not result in a further drop of the biogas H2S concentration. At day 
53, the dosing of air was further increased, which resulted in a H2S

3.3. Case Study #3 
Air injected into the digester resulted in a drop in the biogas H2S 
concentration also within one week, from about 2300 ppmv to about 400 
ppmv. During the next six weeks, the air injection rate was kept constant 
at about 5.1 m3 h−1, which maintained the H2S concentration in the 
biogas at 200–400 ppmv, with the lowest H2S concentration measured 
being 153 ppmv (Fig. 3). The average H2S reduction was 87 % ± 3 % 
when compared with the control digester which was operated similarly 
but without MA. 
The pH of the sludge was 7.25 ± 0.09 without pH control, while the 
operational temperature was kept on average at 37.5 ± 0.2 ◦C. The 
digested sludge during the test period showed a TS content of 2.5 ± 0.03 
% (w/w) and a VS content that was 72 ± 1.2 % of TS. 
On day 16 and day 63 the air injection was stopped for 24 h, which 
directly resulted in the H2S concentration in the biogas rapidly reaching 
the values recorded in the biogas produced in the control digester. 
Directly after resuming the air inject the following day, the H2S reduc­
tion in the biogas was 67 % after about 6 h and 87 % after 24 h. Another 
upset test where the sludge gas mixing blower was turned off for 18 h 
(while air injection was still running) did not negatively affect the H2S 
concentration in the biogas (data not shown). 
3.4. Sulfur conversion 
Dissolved sulfide in the sludge under oxygen-limiting (micro-aero­
bic) conditions is partially oxidized to elemental sulfur, which seems to 
be a stable end-product of the MA process [26,21,23]. This was 
confirmed in all case studies when, after stopping the air injection, the 
H2S concentrations returned to their original values (before staring MA), 
indicating that the produced sulfur product remains stable and no 
elevated biogas H2S concentrations can be expected beyond their orig­
inal values when MA is suddenly stopped. 
The sludge feed, the digested product and the biogas were sampled 
and analyzed for the different sulfur constituents in Case Study #2 to 
generate a sulfur mass balance (Fig. 4). More than 80 % of the sulfur 
entered the digester as organically bound sulfur or elemental sulfur, 
~10 % as sulfate, ~7.5 % as inorganic sulfide precipitants (with metal 
ions) and ~1 % as dissolved sulfide. Inside the digester the sulfate is 
reduced to below detection limits and the total amount of elemental 
sulfur is increased, while the inorganic sulfide precipitants remain un­
changed. The results confirmed that the sulfur that normally left the 
digester as H2S via the biogas, does leave the digester via the solid phase 
of the digested sludge under MA condition when the air is injected into 
the liquid phase. 
Both large-scale tests confirmed the results obtained in bench-scale 
studies [22,8,23], where MA stimulated the activity of sulfide- 
oxidizing bacteria, so that elemental sulfur was formed from the par­
tial oxidation of H2S as per reaction (1).

4. Discussion 
4.1. Critical process parameters 
The results of the three large-scale case studies were compared with 
application data reported in literature to present an overview of known 
large-scale studies at WRRFs and to critically discuss process parame­
ters. Table 1 shows the applications of MA in large-scale digesters re­
ported in literature and includes the three case studies herein 
investigated. The overview shows the different large-scale applications 
including digester size, organic feed material, digester mixing method, 
typical biogas H2S concentrations without MA and H2S reduction ob­
tained under micro-aerobic conditions. 
In general, 80 to over 95 % of H2S reductions have been achieved in 
large-scale applications, some of which have been in operation for 
multiple years [11]. The air may be injected in the sludge feed, recir­
culated sludge or the digester headspace. Most large-scale studies used 
MA injection in the sludge recirculation pipe used for either sludge 
heating or sludge mixing. Although sludge mixing may be accomplished 
through mechanical mixing, for example, sludge recirculation pumps or 
paddle mixers, it may also involve gas mixing, where biogas is being 
recirculated from the headspace to the bottom of the digester reactor.

Although most of the tested digesters were operated under mesophilic

Table 2 shows details of the digester sludge loading rates and MA 
injection methods including air injection rates for the different large- 
scale MA studies mentioned in Table 1. Most large-scale MA applica­
tions involve air injection into the sludge liquid, but injection in the 
digester headspace has also been proven to be effective in large-scale 
applications [29,12]. Air injection in the bottom of the digester tested 
in Case Study #2 was less effective than when the air was injected in the 
sludge recirculation stream similarly to the study described by Cesca and 
co-workers [30]. This was postulated to be caused by the lower oxygen 
transfer efficiency rather than by the MA injection location. 
Different bench-scale studies have been performed to determine the 
optimal oxygen dosage rate at low and high H2S concentrations, mainly 
using oxygen dosage in the headspace of the digester reactor. The 
optimal sulfide removal efficiency can be expected to be about 1 % (v/v) 
of pure O2 per volume of biogas when treating medium to high H2S 
concentrations (i.e., 3300 ppmv) [18]. Nevertheless, the amount of air to 
be dosed seems to be dependent on multiple factors and not only the 
biogas H2S concentration. From the large-scale MA studies reported 
herein, the following general guidelines for large-scale micro-aerobic 
digestion were obtained:  
• Air dosing rate (ambient air) required is typically between 1 and 8 % 
of the biogas flow rate.  
• Air dosing rate (ambient air) required is typically between 0.1 and 
1.75 L h−1 per m3 reactor.  
• Air dosing should provide at least 2.5 times the stoichiometric 
amount of O2 required for the partial H2S oxidation to elemental 
sulfur.  
• More than 90 % H2S removal can be obtained typically when the 
specific biogas production rate of the digester is up to 0.4 Nm3 biogas 
per day per m3 reactor. Higher digestion activities seem to result in a 
lower biogas desulfurization efficiency as illustrated in Fig. 5. The 
digestion activity is affected by organic loading rate and hydraulic 
retention time which could be also parameters influencing desul­
furization efficiency. Similarly, digesters fed with only primary 
sludge are more active with a higher competition for oxygen from the 
injected air, which may lower the biogas desulfurization efficiency 
(see Table 1, Large-scale MA Study #13). The oxygen transfer rate 
efficiency of the MA air injection could also be affected by the 
volumetric biogas production rate (i.e., gas bubble formation rate in 
sludge liquid).  
• Keeping the oxygen dosage below 17 kg O2 per ton VS should not 
upset the digestion process.  
• While MA can be applied in digesters using liquid pump mixing, gas 
mixing and paddle mixing, the sludge mixing intensity and method 
may be highly critical in relation to MA performance and/or the MA 
injection point. Discontinuous mixing (1 h on/1 h off as tested in 
Case Study #1) showed to significantly impact the MA performance 
(see Section 3.2 herein). Moreover, recent MA testing in a full-scale 
donut-type of digester showed that biogas desulfurization was not 
good possible when injecting MA air at the heat sludge recirculation 
pipe which recirculated the sludge in the outer part of the digester, 
while fresh sludge was fed to the inner part of the digester (data not 
shown here).  
• Air injection seems best relatively close to the feedstock injection 
point. 
4.2. Microbial contemplations 
MA provides trace amounts of oxygen for facultative microbes that 
consume and partially reduce oxygen levels [14] in synergistic in­
teractions between facultative and anaerobic microorganisms [26]. The 
concentration of dissolved oxygen present in the sludge is negligible as it 
is quickly and completely consumed during the MA process. Only part of 
the injected oxygen is utilized for the oxidation of dissolved sulfur while 
the rest is utilized by other facultative microbes to oxidize readily 
biodegradable organic matter or leaves the digester as residual oxygen 
in the biogas. It has been shown that the overall digestion process can be 
improved by MA due to a more diverse microbial community that may 
evolve during MA, which may also enhance the hydrolysis processes 
(typically the rate limiting step in anaerobic digesters). In a micro- 
aerated anaerobic process, an environment may be created that main­
tains opportunities for both anaerobic and micro-aerobic facultative 
microbes. Some strict anaerobes can survive and thrive without any 
inhibition when the injected oxygen levels are low [31]. In addition, 
under certain microaerobic conditions, several strict anaerobes have

During anaerobic digestion several interdependent biochemical 
processes are required to produce biogas, which are sensitive, especially 
to high organic loading rates. The anaerobic process involves a series of 
interdependent biochemical steps i.e., hydrolysis, acidogenesis, syntro­
phic acetogenesis, and methanogenesis carried out by diverse microbial 
groups. These interactions between microbes enable organic material 
degradation including some thermodynamically less favorable reactions 
[14]. Anaerobic digestion can be an unstable process, due to the 
disparity between the acetogenic bacteria and methanogens, resulting in 
VFA accumulation, or other process instability often resulting in foam 
formation. Testing of typical potential up-set scenarios of the MA pro­
cess in the digesters in our three full-scale studies did not negatively 
affect the anaerobic digestion process. The VFA/alkalinity ratio as well 
as the biogas production stayed stable in these upset tests. Micro- 
aeration may not only promote sulfide oxidation to reduce H2S in 
biogas but may also enhance the hydrolysis and fermentation of organic 
matter. Micro-aerobic conditions may facilitate aerobic VFA oxidation 
by heterotrophs and may be a strategy to mitigate the inhibitory effects 
caused by accumulating intermediates, thus facilitating the overall sta­
bility of anaerobic digestion processes. The full-scale tests herein 
confirm bench-scale experiments that micro-aerobic conditions may 
therefore also be a simple solution to enhance anaerobic process stability 
[13,15,21,33]. 
Controlling or optimizing the trace amount of oxygen in the digester 
could be paramount. The ORP can sense very small changes in oxygen 
concentrations and could be a control parameter for MA. Monitoring the 
ORP as a parameter to regulate micro-oxygen injection into anaerobic 
digesters for reducing H2S concentration in biogas has been proposed by 
Nghiem and co-workers [24]. ORP varies linearly with the logarithmic 
of the oxygen concentrations. Methane production will occur when the 
ORP is −200 mV or less and acid formation (fermentation with potential 
volatile fatty acid accumulation inhibiting methanogenic activity) will 
mainly occur when the ORP ranges between −75 and −225 mV, while 
micro-aerobic digestion can be defined by the ORP range between 0 mV 
and −300 mV [14]. 
In Case Study #2, ORP-measurements were performed after opti­
mization of the type of probe and location of the probe. Successful 
relatively stable measurements were obtained for several weeks with an 
online ORP meter (HACH) tested in the bypass line of the sludge 
recirculation pump. The results of the online measurements are shown 
in Fig. 6. Fig. 6a shows the results of the ORP measurement taken every 
15 min, Fig. 6b shows the ORP measurement results averaged over 1 h, 
while Fig. 6c shows the ORP measurements averaged over a 4-hour 
period. The 1-hour and 4-hour average would average out the mea­
surements taken every 15 min to reduce the ‘noise’ within the results of 
this very sensitive measurement. A 4-hour average data point was found 
to be sufficient to potentially provide a feedback loop control to the 
amount of air injected as the digestion process is relatively slow and with 
biogas being recirculated within the digested every ~4 h on average. 
Despite relatively stable ORP measurements were obtained with the 
Hach ORP transmitter installed in the sludge pump bypass line, the ORP 
sensor did not provided a direct response when air injection rates were 
changed. In addition, the ORP probe still had to be cleaned frequently as 
debris slowly accumulated on the probe, which render it not reliable 
enough to serve as a control parameter for the MA process. Rather being 
a control parameter the ORP may still be a useful monitoring parameter 
for the MA process, without any control function. All three Case Studies 
showed that, when the digester is fed and operated in a constant manner, 
a constant air injection rate during long-term operation can provide a 
stable H2S desulfurization process without any direct control.

Several typical digestion or micro-aeration process changes or upset 
scenarios were investigated to gain an improved understanding of the 
reliability of the micro-aerobic digestion process. A sudden stop of the 
air injection (all Case Studies) showed that the H2S levels in biogas 
rapidly returned to their original values (before MA). When re-starting 
air injection the H2S concentration dropped within a day to its value 
before stopping the air injection. When air injection rate was overdosed 
(Case Study #1), the VFA/Alkalinity ratio increased first, followed by a 
slight drop in pH the next day and a reduced methane production during 
the following days. While the air injection was left off, within 3 days the 
pH recovered to its original value, while full recovery of the methane 
production took longer: about 5 days to 90 % and about 10 days to 100 
% recovery. A 2-hour sludge recycle pump failure followed by a digester 
feed pump stop for 18 h (Case Study #3) did not cause a decrease in the 
efficiency of biogas desulfurization. The understanding of the reliability 
of the process can provide deeper understanding of the MA process and 
may provide valuable input into the design of permanent large-scale MA 
in terms of instrumentation, monitoring, and automated process 
controls. 
4.3. Safety considerations 
The AD process is typically strictly anaerobic because of the potential 
inhibition in growth and activity of methanogens. Moreover, anaerobic 
conditions are maintained as the addition of oxygen to biogas has a risk 
of explosion at elevated oxygen concentrations. The upper explosion 
limit (UEL, fuel-rich) and lower explosion limits (LEL, fuel-lean) are 
referred to as the mole fractions of the biogas in air at which flame 
propagation after spark ignition no longer occurs. The range between 
the lower and upper explosion limits is known as explosion range, which 
depends on the biogas composition, and is typically between 5 % (v/v) 
and 25 % (v/v). Methane leaking from process units into the ambient air 
environment should be the main concern regarding the formation of an 
explosive atmosphere at WRRFs. Micro-aerobic digestion on the other 
hand operates at an oxygen-to-biogas ratio robustly lower than that 
required to reach the upper flammability limit of biogas/air mixtures. 
Nevertheless, control/safety strategies need to be implemented to 
maintain safe operations of large-scale digesters operated under micro- 
aerobic conditions. 
To eliminate any risks both intrinsic measures and extrinsic measures 
are proposed here. Intrinsic measures are features inherent of the pro­
cess which can't be changed during its operation and may be an orifice 
and air fuse as part of the MA air supply system. Extrinsic measures are 
additional features to the process controls and may be air injection 
control interlocks with feedback from equipment/instruments. The 
control of air injection stops as it interlocks for example with the sludge 
recirculation flow interruption, any gas recirculation interruption, any 
sludge feed interruptions and/or too high oxygen concentrations in 
biogas. While the extrinsic measures should be robust controls, the 
intrinsic are the basic line of defense against unsafe conditions 
independent on instruments and instrument feedback loops, and inde­
pendent of power availability. 
4.4. High-level comparison with conventional biogas desulfurization 
technologies 
Table 3 shows a high-level comparison of MA with conventional 
biogas desulfurization methods including ferric chloride dosing and end- 
of-pipe systems such as dry media adsorbents, iron coated media (e.g., 
iron sponge) or wet scrubbing systems. The comparison shows some of 
the important considerations when using the different methods, ad­
vantages and disadvantages and general capital and operational costs 
based on existing facilities. 
The potential capital and operational cost savings that MA technol­
ogy could provide are substantial. The capital cost for an end-of-pipe 
biogas desulfurization technology varies depending on the biogas flow 
rate and inlet H2S concentration. This can be well over one million 
dollars installed for a typical mid-size WRRF - while the capital cost of a 
MA system is estimated to be about $250,000. These are in line with the 
economic analysis of microaerobic in large-scale sludge digesters as 
described by Diaz and c-workers [9]. Moreover, the operational cost of 
MA is negligible compared to end-of-pipe technologies, which may 
require input of chemicals such as caustic, activated carbon or iron- 
based material, etc. [34], while MA eliminates the disposal of the 
typical end-products for these end-of-pipe technologies. This includes 
sulfuric acid, elemental sulfur slurry or spent iron oxide–based adsor­
bents and extra sludge requiring disposal in the case of ferric chloride 
dosing. 
Conventional measures are typically in place in digestion facilities at 
wastewater facilities to reduce the H2S in biogas, but they require sig­
nificant ongoing costs and could be improved in terms of sustainability 
(e.g., iron dosing requiring ongoing input of chemicals or end-of-pipe 
systems like coated dry media system such as iron sponge or impreg­
nated activated carbon media requiring frequent replacement and 
disposal of the spent media typical to landfill). In many of these cases 
can MA provide large benefits in terms of cost savings and environ­
mental benefits (less chemical usage, less input of raw materials, lower 
energy cost, lower carbon footprint). In those cases that MA provides 
cannot reduce the H2S concentrations low enough, the existing systems 
can still be used as polishing while MA is providing the bulk of the effort 
in terms of biogas desulfurization. 
MA can provide high biogas desulfurization efficiencies (>95 %) as 
illustrated in Fig. 5, but microbial activity inside the digester (expressed 
in the volumetric biogas formation rate) is relevant, which can provide 
guidance for what efficiencies are feasible with MA (or could also be 
used as guide to design or set digester loading rates for when MA is to be 
implemented). Further polishing of the biogas may, in certain cases, still 
be required when applying MA depending on the H2S concentration 
level in the biogas and the downstream processing of the biogas (e.g., 
upgrading to biomethane).

A potential drawback of micro-aeration could be the risk of diluting 
the methane concentration excessively such that the biogas is too lean 
for proper combustion. Alternatively, concentrated or pure oxygen 
rather than air may be used as demonstrated by Diaz and coworkers 
[29], especially when biogas is upgraded to biomethane, because ni­
trogen is an inert gas very difficult to remove from the biogas during 
upgrading to biomethane. 
The accumulation of elemental sulfur in the digester headspace or 
downstream process units such as flame arrestors might potentially 
cause operational problems. Long-term (one year or more) operation of 
MA can result in elemental sulfur deposition on flame arrestors requiring 
more frequent cleaning as have been observed in the digesters described 
in Case Study #2 after the MA process for about 2 years after the study. 
Cleaning and maintenance would demand a dual arrangement at any 
pressure relief valve (PRV) and flame arrestors. This drawback of MA 
can be managed by installing dual PRV arrangements when micro- 
aeration is implemented and should be combined with additional 
instrumentation (especially air injection monitoring and oxygen moni­
toring in the biogas). 
5. Conclusions 
Micro-aerobic digestion studies in three different large-scale di­
gesters at WRRFs were conducted and the results support bench-scale 
research performed to date that micro-aeration technology holds po­
tential as an effective and more sustainable biogas desulfurization 
method compared to conventional biogas desulfurization technologies. 
A sulfur balance over a full-scale sludge digestion process was success­
fully obtained. This, together with micro-aerobic process interruption 
tests showed that a stable end-product (elemental sulfur) is formed in 
the liquid phase, which leaves the digester via the solid phase of the 
digested sludge when air is injected into the liquid phase. The air in­
jection rate and the air injection location as well as the volumetric 
biogas production rate showed to be important parameters affecting the 
micro-aerobic desulfurization performance in large-scale digesters. The 
need to a process parameter for automated control (e.g., ORP) seems not 
requisite for the MA process in large-scale sludge digesters at WRRFs. 
Reliability testing of typical upset scenarios and long-term micro-aero­
bic digester operation provided deeper insights in the MA process that 
could also provide valuable input to what operational, maintenance and 
safety measures should be considered when applying micro-aeration in 
large-scale digesters.
